Diomedes.fact: This speech signifies the nature of Homeric tradition where fate and divine interventions have superiority over human choices.

Diomedes.subject: World Geography

Diomedes.fact: Nestor believed in the importance of human choices and proposed to change Achilles' mind by offering many gifts. The embassy failed because Achilles himself had more faith in his own choices than fate or divine interventions.

Diomedes.fact: He threatened to leave Troy, never to return believing that this choice will enable him to live a long life. Diomedes.fact: During the Achaean council held, Agamemnon asked for a volunteer to spy on the Trojans.

Diomedes.fact: Finally Hector managed to send Dolon, a good runner, after making a false oath (promising him Achilles' horses after the victory).

Diomedes.fact: If we set you free tonight, there is nothing to prevent your coming down once more to the Achaean ships, either to play the spy or to meet us in open fight.

Diomedes.fact: They took the spoils and set them upon a tamarisk tree in honour of Athena.

Diomedes.fact: Meanwhile, Odysseus gathered the team of Rhesus' horses.

Diomedes.fact: He was planning to kill more Thracians and steal the chariot of the king with his armour when Athena advised him to retire, lest some other god might warn the Trojans.

Diomedes.subject: World Geography

Diomedes.fact: Another version (Virgil and Servius) says that Rhesus was given an oracle that claims he will be invincible after he and his horses drink from the Scamander.

Diomedes.fact: This throw was accurate but the helmet given by Apollo saved Hector's life.

Diomedes.fact: Hector soon marked the havoc Diomedes and Odysseus were making, and approached them. Diomedes immediately threw his spear at Hector, aiming for his head.

Diomedes.fact: Moreover, the goddess spoke to the hero without any disguise in Book V where he could see her in the true divine form (a special vision was granted to him).

Diomedes.fact: Penthesileia killed many Achaeans in battle.

Earthquake.question: The seismicity at a particular location in the _____ is the average rate of seismic energy release per unit volume
Earthquake.fact: An earthquake, also called a quake, tremor, or temblor, is the shaking of the Earth's surface resulting from a sudden release of energy in the lithosphere that creates seismic waves.  Earthquakes can range in intensity, from those so weak they cannot be felt, to those violent enough to propel objects and people into the air, damage critical infrastructure, and wreak destruction across entire cities.  The seismic activity of an area is the frequency, type, and size of earthquakes experienced over a particular time.  The seismicity at a particular location in the Earth is the average rate of seismic energy released per unit volume.  In its most general sense, the word earthquake is used to describe any seismic event that generates seismic waves.  Earthquakes can occur naturally or be induced by human activities, such as mining, fracking, and nuclear weapons testing.  The initial point of rupture is called the hypocenter or focus, while the ground level directly above it is the epicenter

Rocks hotter than about 300 °C (572 °F) flow in response to stress; they do not rupture in earthquakes.  The maximum observed lengths of ruptures and mapped faults (which may break in a single rupture) are approximately 1,000 km (620 mi). Earthquake.fact: In the event of water mains rupturing and a loss of pressure, it may also become difficult to stop the spread of a fire once it has started.  For example, more deaths in the 1906 San Francisco earthquake were caused by fire than by the earthquake itself.  === Tsunami === Tsunamis are long-wavelength, long-period sea waves produced by the sudden or abrupt movement of large volumes of water—including when an earthquake occurs at sea.  In the open ocean, the distance between wave crests can surpass 100 kilometres (62 mi), and the wave periods can vary from five minutes to one hour.  Such tsunamis travel 600–800 kilometers per hour (373–497 miles per hour), depending on water depth.  Large waves produced by an earthquake or a submarine landslide can overrun nearby coastal areas in a matter of minutes.
